name: Distinction Bias
description: Small differences between options feel larger when the options are compared side by side than when each is experienced on its own. Comparison mode can manufacture importance that disappears in real use.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to pricing tables, feature-comparison pages, marketplace sorting, benchmark dashboards, and stakeholder reviews that over-index on side-by-side spec differences users will barely notice in lived experience.
prevalence_note: Recognized in behavioral-product and pricing discussions, especially around comparison tables, but not a staple named concept in general UX curricula.

findings.description: A series of experiments found evaluators were more likely to base hiring/promotion decisions on actual individual performance when candidates were evaluated jointly rather than separately, and more likely to rely on group stereotypes (introducing gender bias) when evaluated separately. Joint evaluation functioned as an effective 'evaluation nudge' reducing gender-biased hiring decisions -- a genuine, high-stakes, real-world application of the same joint-vs-separate evaluation mechanism behind distinction bias, extending it from consumer product judgments into hiring and promotion decisions.
findings.source_title: When Performance Trumps Gender Bias: Joint vs. Separate Evaluation

findings.description: How attractive a product looks depends on evaluation mode: side-by-side comparison makes attribute differences loom larger than they do in isolated evaluation, so the same option can be judged more or less attractive simply because it is presented jointly rather than separately.
findings.source_title: Will Products Look More Attractive When Presented Separately Or Together?
